JSON: Name: feedback_mppi_pipeline Title: Computing local linear feedback gains via rollout differentiation to provide high-frequency inner-loop corrections for sampling-based MPC in nonlinear robotic control Short Hypothesis: Applying local linear feedback gains computed by differentiating MPPI rollouts and using them in a high-frequency inner-loop reduces closed-loop tracking error and control action variance compared to standard MPPI given the same overall computational budget. Related Work: Sampling-based MPC (MPPI) enables control for highly nonlinear and non-convex robotic tasks by evaluating many stochastic rollouts in parallel, but its closed-loop rate is limited by computational cost and rollout noise, which can cause oscillations and degraded tracking. Gradient-based MPC and DDP methods obtain efficient time-varying linear feedback (Riccati) gains via sensitivity analysis or backward recursion, enabling high-frequency inner-loop control but relying on local linearization and often requiring access to analytic derivatives or heavy solver iterations. Approaches that directly approximate MPC policies (e.g., learned networks with online sensitivity corrections) reduce runtime but need offline training and may struggle to generalize across operating regimes. Existing remedies for MPPI include GPU acceleration, filtering, and learned importance sampling to improve stability or throughput; these do not produce explicit local feedback gains. Limitations across prior work include: (1) trade-offs between global nonconvex search and inner-loop responsiveness; (2) reliance on full re-optimization for feedback in sampling methods; (3) difficulty handling input saturation and non-differentiable constraints in rollout-based sensitivity computation; and (4) limited demonstrations of combining sampling-based global optimization with locally derived Riccati-like gains for real hardware under strict onboard compute constraints. Abstract: We propose a structured pipeline that augments sampling-based Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control with local linear feedback gains computed by differentiating rollout costs with respect to the current state. The pipeline computes sensitivity-informed gains from the MPPI solution using automatic differentiation of parallel rollouts, then applies those gains in a high-frequency inner-loop around a nominal trajectory, reducing the need to re-solve the full stochastic optimization at each control tick. The main contribution is the integration of rollout-differentiated Riccati-like gains into an MPPI framework, preserving MPPI's ability to handle nonlinear, non-convex objectives while providing faster closed-loop responsiveness and smoother actions. The pipeline is applicable to mixed continuous and hybrid dynamics and explicitly specifies experimental protocols for simulation and hardware validation on legged and aerial robots. Expected outcomes include statistically significant reductions in tracking error and action variance under matched computational budgets, enabling more stable and higher-frequency control on embedded platforms without modifying the global sampling architecture. Experiments: Environments and platforms: (1) Quadruped: Aliengo2 dynamics in MuJoCo for simulation and Unitree Aliengo2 hardware tests; (2) Quadrotor: MikroKopter model in Gazebo and real vehicle running Telekyb3 on an Nvidia Jetson Orin NX; (3) Hybrid test: 1D Hopper simulated in MJX/MuJoCo with contact switching; (4) Obstacle navigation: Gazebo environment with static circular obstacles and motion-capture-style state estimation for quadrotor. Baselines: (A) Standard MPPI executing at maximum frequency available on the target hardware (no gains); (B) MPPI adjusted to match the CPU/GPU time budget of the proposed method (higher samples or lower frequency as appropriate); (C) Gradient-based MPC with Riccati inner-loop (when linearizable) or DDP re-solver; (D) Learned policy imitation of MPPI (if available) with no online sensitivity correction. Controller configurations: use cubic/linear spline parametrization, horizon N ∈ {5,10,15}, timestep δt as in target platform (quadruped 0.02 s, quadrotor 0.05 s), sample counts K ∈ {400,800,1200,5000} depending on platform, and noise/disturbance injection (Gaussian state disturbance and external forces up to specified amplitudes). Trials: 50 randomized trials per configuration with different seeds. Evaluation metrics: positional RMSE (x,y,z), velocity RMSE, action variance (per-axis variance and power spectral density aggregated into a smoothness score), success rate (reach goal without collision or falling), number of constraint violations (contacts outside friction cone, clipped inputs), computation time per control cycle (mean, median, 95th percentile), maximum latency, and energy proxy (sum of squared inputs). Statistical analysis: report mean ± std and perform paired significance tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank) between proposed method and each baseline. Ablation studies: (1) proposed MPPI gains vs MPPI without gains at matched computation time; (2) gains computed using linearized rollouts vs nonlinear rollouts; (3) gains computed with rollout differentiation but with/without input clipping during rollouts; (4) effect of varying K and N on performance and compute time; (5) CPU-only vs GPU-accelerated implementations. Success criteria: statistically significant reduction in positional RMSE and action variance for the proposed method relative to baseline MPPI within the same computational budget. Risk Factors and Limitations: Differentiability requirement: the gains rely on rollout cost gradients; non-differentiable dynamics, hard discontinuities from contact or discontinuous costs can make gradients meaningless or misleading. Input clipping and active inequality constraints: when many rollouts saturate inputs, the partial derivatives of the parametrization may vanish, degrading gain signals. Hybrid dynamics and mode switches: first-order feedback gains computed around sampled trajectories may not capture discrete mode transitions and can become invalid near contact creation/removal. Computational overhead: computing rollout derivatives increases per-cycle latency and may limit achievable closed-loop frequency on resource-constrained hardware; benefits depend on available parallel compute and may not hold when GPU cores are saturated. Generalization and robustness: locally computed gains may only be valid in a neighborhood of the nominal trajectory and can fail under large disturbances or model mismatch. Numerical stability: backpropagation through long horizons can suffer from gradient vanishing/explosion or numerical noise leading to poor gain estimates. Safety and constraint handling: rollout-derived gains do not inherently enforce hard constraints; unsafe control actions may arise if rollouts poorly explore collision-free trajectories. Evaluation bias: results may be sensitive to chosen cost weights, sampling distributions, and randomized seeds; positive results on specific robots/environments may not transfer broadly without retuning.
